transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-08-15
Time: 16:00 UTC / 09:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Ellis (Riverbend CTO), Sofia Reyes (Product), Evan Brooks (DevOps), Lina Park (Security)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on Riverbend's privacy-first constraints and options between Redwood hosted API (fastest path) vs Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private VPC/on-prem. Customer wants to understand time-to-first-token under PLG/self-serve, free credits, and the lift for a privacy-constrained pilot. Security requirements (KMS, SSO, audit logs, data residency) drove most questions. SE covered caching, batching, quantization tradeoffs and suggested a short benchmark/PoC.

Topics:
- Current stack and data flows
- Privacy & residency requirements
- Time-to-first-token for a PLG onramp
- Dedicated vs hosted vs private deployment tradeoffs
- Pilot success metrics and roles

Highlight links shared during call:
- Quickstart guide: https://redwood.example/quickstart
- Security pack (placeholder link): https://redwood.example/security-pack
- Benchmark template (sheet): https://redwood.example/benchmarks/rb-template

Action items (recap at end): see action_items field above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intro we got about 45 minutes, is that still good for folks?
[00:05] Mark Ellis: yep that's perfect. morning Alex. thanks.
[00:07] Priya Nair: hi team, i'm priya on the infra side, i'll walk a bit through latency/cost tradeoffs during the call.
[00:12] Sofia Reyes: hey all, quick note i'm mostly product thinking about where the assistant will live in our app.
[00:16] Evan Brooks: devops here, we'll need to know networking and egress.
[00:18] Lina Park: security, will ask about keys and retention.

[00:22] Alex Chen: great. high level — redwood offers hosted API for fastest time to first token, dedicated pools for predictable throughput, and private (vpc or on-prem) for strict privacy. curious — where are you in the evaluation? quick summary from your side, mark?
[00:35] Mark Ellis: sure. Riverbend is building an analyst assistant on top of internal docs and financial data; PII and some client data are in the corpus. initial goal is prototype within engineering then roll to product. main blocker is client data residency and encryption at rest; we need to know how fast we can stand up something without exposing keys.
[00:55] Alex Chen: totally — good constraints. to confirm: data residency means some datasets must stay in eu-west-1 and be encrypted with your KMS?
[01:03] Mark Ellis: yes EU for a subset of clients, and our security folks insist on customer-managed keys where possible.
[01:08] Priya Nair: ok so that pushes private or dedicated VPC options usually. hosted can work if you use our dedicated or private offering with bring-your-own-key. i can outline the minimal steps.
[01:18] Lina Park: does redwood support HSM or external key providers? we use an HSM-backed KMS for the sensitive buckets.
[01:25] Priya Nair: we integrate with customer KMS via our private control plane — the on-premises package supports HSM integrations; for dedicated in cloud we support BYOK via KMS and CMKs. small caveat: if you want to sign logs or have offline key custody we recommend the private on-prem path.
[01:45] Sofia Reyes: for the quickstart: how long till we can call the API and get a response? we're trying to understand time-to-first-token for PM planning.
[01:53] Alex Chen: good question. for PLG/self-serve hosted it's minutes: create account, get API key, run sample requests. with our free credits we can get you to first meaningful test within a day. for dedicated or private there is extra provisioning — dedicated can be hours to a day depending on capacity, private (VPC) typically a few days for cloud VPC setup, on-prem longer.
[02:12] Evan Brooks: hours to a day for dedicated? what's the common bottleneck there?
[02:15] Priya Nair: mostly networking and capacity pinning — reserving GPU pools, setting up VPC peering, and security onboarding. if you have strict firewall rules we'll need a few firewall exceptions.
[02:26] Evan Brooks: we run strict egress, we prefer to keep inference inside our network if possible.
[02:30] Priya Nair: understood — two paths: 1) private deployment where the inference runtime runs in your VPC or on-prem, 2) or dedicated with private peering and strict ACLs. both keep data inside allowed regions.
[02:40] Mark Ellis: cost question — sounds like private costs more. any ballpark numbers for reserved capacity vs hosted?
[02:46] Alex Chen: rough heuristics — hosted per-token pricing is easiest for prototyping, dedicated reserved capacity gives lower per-token cost at steady scale, private/on-prem has higher fixed ops and infra costs but reduces egress and increases control. we'll send a tailored estimate based on expected qps and token mix.
[03:05] Sofia Reyes: what about model variants — we want a smaller model for cheap quick responses and a larger one for heavy analysis. is switching runtime easy?
[03:12] Priya Nair: yes — our routing abstraction allows policy-based routing by model, latency SLO, or cost. you can pin stages to different model sizes; the console supports gradual rollouts and canary.
[03:22] Mark Ellis: security — audit logs and SSO. we need to prove who saw what and RBAC for dev vs product.
[03:28] Priya Nair: audit logs are standard on dedicated and private, with longer retention optional as an add-on. SSO via SAML/SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC roles in the console.
[03:40] Lina Park: retention policies — can you configure no-logs for certain sessions? we need some calls to be ephemeral.
[03:46] Alex Chen: yes, you can mark requests as non-retained and we have redaction hooks; in private you can fully disable retention. for hosted we offer configurable retention windows and manual redaction APIs.
[03:58] Evan Brooks: priya you mentioned caching and kv cache — how does that interact with PII?
[04:03] Priya Nair: good callout — our KV cache/prefix cache accelerates repeated context. for sensitive keys you can opt out of caching or encrypt cached blobs with customer keys. also we recommend caching only non-sensitive embeddings where possible.
[04:18] Mark Ellis: is kv pronounced kay-vee? we kept saying kay-vee in our team.
[04:21] Priya Nair: laugh it's kay-vee but kay-vee is fine.
[04:25] Sofia Reyes: practical pilot idea — give us credits to try hosted self-serve on non-sensitive data while we test private provisioning for EU clients. sound reasonable?
[04:33] Alex Chen: that's exactly the normal path. free credits for hosted to validate flows and UX, then pilot dedicated/VPC for regulated clients.
[04:38] Mark Ellis: we want benchmarks for latency at 95th pct for a 512 token request. can we get sample numbers?
[04:44] Priya Nair: typical 95th for a 512-token generation on a modern open model in hosted is around 120–300ms depending on model and seq. for dedicated with pinned GPU it's lower and more stable. i'll include a benchmark template and a plan to run the same workload in your environment.
[05:00] Evan Brooks: network needs — what ports and egress endpoints do we need to allow for hosted?
[05:05] Alex Chen: for hosted you'll need egress to api.redwood.example and a few telemetry endpoints; we'll send a minimal allowlist. for private/on-prem it's inbound peering into your VPC.
[05:12] Lina Park: compliance — do you have SOC2 plus any financial-specific attestations?
[05:17] Alex Chen: we have SOC2 Type II and are working through ISO. for financial attestations we can provide architecture diagrams and isolation controls; we'll attach the security pack after the call.
[05:30] Sofia Reyes: ok on the PLG metrics — if we do hosted quickstart, what's the typical TTFT (time-to-first-token) for our PM to demo?
[05:37] Alex Chen: minutes. sign up, create API key, point client and call sample endpoint. with our quickstart sample you can have a working chat within an hour end-to-end including simple auth.
[05:45] Mark Ellis: any red flags with our stack? we're on GCP eu-west-1 and use HashiCorp Vault for secrets.
[05:50] Priya Nair: that's a good fit. we support Vault for secrets sync and have guides for cloud-run and k8s deployments in eu-west-1.
[05:58] Evan Brooks: do you support private endpoint peering into GCP VPC?
[06:02] Alex Chen: yes, private peering for dedicated and private offerings is supported for GCP, AWS, and Azure. setup time depends on your networking team.
[06:10] Mark Ellis: who should own the pilot on our side? product or infra?
[06:14] Sofia Reyes: product will run the UX tests but infra will handle private provisioning. i'll coordinate.
[06:18] Alex Chen: perfect. recommended plan: 1) hosted quickstart with free credits for product to validate flows, 2) SE benchmark run with sample data, 3) provision dedicated/VPC for EU-bound clients.
[06:31] Lina Park: small nit — any data residency guarantees in hosted?
[06:34] Priya Nair: hosted allows region selection for data residency but for strict legal requirements we prefer private or dedicated pinned to the region.
[06:41] Mark Ellis: great. any other questions from you, sophia?
[06:44] Sofia Reyes: curious about tool-calling and structured outputs — can we return JSON with schema enforcement?
[06:50] Priya Nair: yep we support structured output constraints and function/tool calling primitives via the API. schema enforcement is supported with validation hooks in the SDK.
[06:59] Evan Brooks: what's the best way to share sample data for a benchmark without breaking policy?
[07:05] Alex Chen: redact PII and share synthetic or hashed keys; if needed we can run a runbook in your VPC with the SE so nothing leaves your network.
[07:15] Mark Ellis: we'll probably do the VPC-runbook since that removes the residue concern.
[07:20] Alex Chen: makes sense. last item — i'll outline the pilot success metrics so we're aligned. typical ones are: accuracy/top-1 correctness on retrieval tasks, 95th latency under target, token cost per query under budget, and integration work effort.
[07:38] Sofia Reyes: sounds good.
[07:40] Alex Chen: ok let's recap next steps — i'll send security pack and credits, priya will prepare benchmark plan. match the action items above.
[07:50] Mark Ellis: thanks all — solid call.
[07:52] Priya Nair: thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript tone and imperfections: occasional mispronunciations (kay-vee), filler words, overlap and short crosstalk. Some brand names lightly garbled in speech-to-text.
